We found that this behavior results in a higher concentration of plagiarized short phrases directly translated from the source language. To exploit these findings, we introduced a dual-strategy approach, applying both in-language and cross-language detection techniques. Our results showed that this method achieved a significant improvement in accuracy, outperforming existing systems by a large margin. To facilitate further research, we released our dataset containing more than 1 million documents along with their associated features. To address this issue, we incorporated an existing detection system along with our own domain adaptation technique to enhance performance in the new domain. Although our study focused on English and non-English language pairs, our technique is versatile and can be applied to other language combinations. In difficult domains characterized by a lack of similarity between source and target languages, our method achieved the best overall results. We observed a substantial improvement in accuracy when detecting plagiarized passages in difficult domains such as legal and scientific texts. Our code and data are available at https://github.com/ghrua/xl-plagiarism. hysterectomy and uterine embolization as treatments for uterine fibroids, examining the underlying causes and effects of these conditions and their associated treatment methods.  A uterine fibroid is a common condition among women of childbearing age, characterized by the growth of benign tumors in the uterus.  These tumors are made up of smooth muscle cells and fibroblastic cells, and are hormonally sensitive, meaning their growth is triggered by the female hormones estrogen and progesterone.  As a result, they typically shrink after menopause, when hormone production decreases.  There are three main types of fibroids based on location: submucosal, intramural, and subserosal.  Women with intramural fibroids may not experience any symptoms at all, while those with submucosal or subserosal fibroids may experience heavy menstrual bleeding, infertility issues, and gastrointestinal discomfort among other symptoms.  Uterine embolization is a minimally invasive procedure used to treat fibroids and other conditions of the uterus and vagina.  During this procedure, a doctor uses x-ray imaging to guide the injection of small particles into the blood vessels supplying the uterus, cutting off the oxygen and nutrient supply to the fibroids, causing them to shrink.  On the other hand, hysterectomy involves the surgical removal of the uterus, a procedure that is typically considered a last resort for women with fibroids who have not responded to other treatments and are experiencing severe symptoms.  It is worth noting that hysterectomy results in infertility and menopause, while uterine embolization is a reversible procedure that allows women to retain their fertility until they choose to undergo the procedure.  Advances in medical technology, including the development of magnetic resonance imaging, have improved our understanding of fibroids and their treatment, leading to the adoption of less invasive procedures such as uterine embolization and myomectomy.  As a result, hysterectomy is now primarily reserved for older women with larger fibroids who have not responded to other treatments and are experiencing severe symptoms.  In conclusion, uterine embolization and hysterectomy are two treatments for uterine fibroids that have gained prominence in recent years, with uterine embolization emerging as a preferred option for younger women with smaller fibroids and hysterectomy being considered for older women with larger fibroids. reports the results of a nationwide survey in Japan, comparing the accuracy of
three different types of PPG devices.  We conducted a parallel comparison of
these devices using a reference device over a nationwide range of 103 different
locations.  The data consisted of oxygen saturation readings from three pairs
of devices, produced by different manufacturers, and a reference device, using
six subjects at each of these locations.  The study provided a comprehensive
analysis of the data, incorporating spatial and subject variables, to
determine the source of inaccuracy.  Our analysis revealed a high degree of
inconsistency in the results, affected by both spatial and subject factors. 
Several non-linear methods were applied to account for these factors and
predict reference values.  We evaluated several models, including neural networks
and support vector machines, to determine their ability to accurately forecast
reference values.  Validation of the best models was conducted using data
from five subjects and did not produce satisfactory results.  However, when we used
a different approach, we entered the data into a generalized linear mixed model, 
which yielded a high degree of accuracy in forecasting reference values. 
Ultimately, our study indicated that the inaccuracy of these devices cannot be
captured linearly but may be better modeled through a complex interaction of
both spatial and subject variables.  We also found that the inaccuracy is highly
variable and cannot be forecast linearly.  Our study provides a reference for
both the medical and engineering communities, offering a framework that can be
applied to similar accuracy assessment situations.  We suggest that a mixed
effects model is an effective approach to model inaccuracy when it is influenced
by an amalgamation of both fixed and random factors.

When the Ricci scalar is negative and its absolute value is relatively small, the spin's effects are negligible.  However, in scenarios where the Ricci scalar is positive and relatively small, or in cases where it's negative but relatively large, the spin's effects become more significant, resulting in gravitational waves that take longer to complete one cycle and exhibit amplitude variations throughout their journey. In this research, we explore the benefits of natural gradient descent in training a specific type of quantum circuit, specifically the quantum neural network known as Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm.  We demonstrate that natural gradient descent enabled significant reductions in training time and yielded better test accuracies when compared to a constant learning rate optimizer.   In this paper, we explore specific configurations where two Q-balls, either of the same or opposite charges, exist across two scalar fields with a specific symmetry. These particular configurations meet the requirements for stable, rotating Q-balls. When these Q-balls are apart, our model indicates that they can exist safely, and our numerical simulations demonstrate that they can even move at consistent speeds. Additionally, our findings show that when these Q-balls collide, either with the same charge or with opposite charges, a unique and complex interaction occurs, resulting in a combination of scalar wave disturbances and a local distortion of space-time. This leads to a transient formation of an Einstein-Rosen wormhole linking the two Q-balls, and this phenomenon occurs instantaneously across space-time. This happens both when the Q-balls have the same charge, where they become permanently connected, as well as when they have opposite charges. In the latter case, there is also a possibility of matter exchange through this wormhole. This occurs because the interface between two Q-balls with opposite charges can become unstable, giving rise to a stable, though dynamic, configuration. This dynamic configuration can also occur with more than two Q-balls, given that they are all properly charged and aligned, and it may provide a mechanism for the creation of Einstein-Rosen wormholes. This could be particularly relevant in situations involving multiple scalar fields and their interconnecting Q-balls. This study explores the Stokes lines, or the loci of such behavior, for the Airy function $\Ai(z)$ in the complex plane. These lines originate from the singularities of $\Ai(z)$ and converge to directions defined by the angles of the complex plane. Near the line corresponding to an angle of $\frac{5\pi}{3}$, the Stokes line exhibits unique behavior, forming a wedge within the line determined by the coordinates $(1, -1)$ in the complex plane. This study aims to identify the boundary of the Stokes lines for $\Ai(z)$ with $z=0$ as a singularity, specifically mapping the boundary in the direction of $\frac{5\pi}{3}$ for the first time. This problem has been previously shown to be solvable when the tree $T$ is a path. In this research, we demonstrate that if the tree $T$ contains a leaf node with a degree greater than 1, then there will always be a solution. Conversely, if the tree $T$ does not contain any leaf nodes with a degree greater than 1, then there may not always be a solution. This has led to the classification of trees into two categories: 'good' trees, which include paths and trees with at least one leaf node with a degree greater than 1, and 'bad' trees, which do not contain any leaf nodes with a degree greater than 1. The notion of assigning the same number to nodes that have the same level of ancestry is then further generalized to a concept called $k$-symmetric sets. We demonstrate that, due to the absence of nonlinear phenomena such as wave breaking and the supply of energy from deeper layers, there is no limitation on the duration of time over which the linearized equations are applicable. We present a new method for solving the linearized equations of a finite periodic domain and demonstrate that a finite-time "glowing string" solution exists. We observe that this solution can be realized experimentally. We also show that our approach can be used to investigate highly irregular patterns that form over a very long period of time. Due to the instantaneity of the wave's response to changes, its speed, and the geometry of the domain, certain patterns that form through modulation instability lead to the creation of multiple "glowing string" solutions. These solutions correspond to the propagation of waves in different layers of the domain. We demonstrate that these solutions interact with each other through the generation of rarefactions. These interactions can cause the "glowing string" solution to transition into another state. This transition is an example of mode resonance. It occurs when the wave's response to a perturbation becomes indirect, due to another wave that propagates at a different speed and in a different layer being affected. We also demonstrate that a finite-time "glowing string" solution can be realized if a specific type of wave, which we call a "resonant wave", exists. This type of wave has a response to perturbations that is a combination of direct and indirect effects. Due to the instantaneity of its response to changes in its layer, a resonant wave can propagate over a very long period of time. We demonstrate that another type of wave, which we call a "non-resonant wave", has an indirect response to perturbations in its layer. This type of wave cannot create a "glowing string" solution. However, a non-resonant wave can be created from a resonant wave in another layer through the generation of rarefactions. This paper reports on the most extreme magnetic field ever observed, which was found in the environment surrounding a GRB.  To make this discovery, researchers used the Faraday rotation technique with data from the MAGIC telescope.  Specifically, they analyzed observations from GRB 191109BC, which showed an excess Faraday rotation compared to expectations, indicating the presence of a highly magnetized plasma.  Modeling this effect revealed the magnetic field to have a strength of around 106 Gauss, which is incredibly high and only a few percent of the maximum possible energy observed in the universe.  This finding suggests the environment surrounding GRBs can create strong magnetic fields through the interaction of relativistic pluses with the host star's magnetic field.  Further studies are needed to understand how this affects the observed properties of GRBs.  It is also worth noting that this detection was made possible due to the low energy threshold of the MAGIC telescope, which allowed for the observation of a GRB at such a great distance.  As a result of this discovery, there is a new potential use for the technique of Faraday rotation in gamma-ray astrophysics, which could be used to study the magnetized plasmas surrounding GRBs and other gamma-ray sources.  Furthermore, it is also possible that this technique could be employed to search for signatures of magnetic fields in the early universe, which could have a profound impact on our understanding of the universe's magnetic field.  As for the environment surrounding GRBs, it is now also possible to use this technique to study the plasma surrounding these explosions in different wavelengths.  As a result of this discovery, there is also a need to update and improve the plasma models used to simulate the interaction of GRBs with their surroundings, which could have a significant impact on our ability to accurately predict the observed properties of GRBs through simulation.  As a result of this discovery, there is also a new potential for observations to be made with the MAGIC telescope, which could result in the detection of more excess Faraday rotation in the environment surrounding a GRB, which in turn could result in the discovery of more extreme magnetic fields in the universe.   To address this limitation, our proposed Hybrid-RCNN framework mitigates the need for proposal extraction.

Networks in various media, such as photos, videos, and audio, the challenge of detecting naturally occurring deep-faked content has become increasingly important. Although existing research primarily focuses on detecting deep-faked visual and audio content, little work has been done on discovering deep-faked text, particularly in the context of coherent language generation. To address this gap, we propose a new Text Detection Module (TDModule) that identifies artificially created coherent text within conversation histories. TDModule uses a conversation-aware approach, leveraging both the textual characteristics of the Markovian structure and the statistical model used to generate the text. It achieves this by training two distinct sets of detectors: one for the generator's syntactic patterns and another for the underlying probability models. Additionally, TDModule includes an auxiliary classifier that identifies the generator's structural markers and incorporates both sets of detectors to produce the final detection outcome. We evaluated our approach on the recent RedAdventures dataset, introducing an additional downsampled version of the data, known as RedAdv-16k. Our results demonstrate that our proposed TDModule module surpasses the current state-of-the-art techniques and exhibits consistent performance improvements on both the full (50k data subset) and the smaller (16k data subset) versions of the provided data categories. The analysis of our approach and the comprehensive discussion of the challenges encountered in this project are also included. Furthermore, we make our source code and data available for public use. This method has been the dominant approach for over a century, with its shortcomings only recently subject to thorough analysis.  We take a step back from holding data apart and explore an alternative inspired by the theory of robust optimization.  We present a general framework that can be applied to any statistical model and data distribution. We also examine the conditions under which this method produces results similar to the traditional approach. Within their framework, they identified necessary conditions for optimality, expressed as a combination of maximum principles and transversality conditions applied to a modified value function. The value function, a key concept in their analysis, is defined as the sum of the present discounted costs of future state and control trajectories. The state and control trajectories themselves are subject to linear time-invariant differential equations. The purpose of the study is to explore alternatives to their polynomial-decay assumption, specifically examining the implications of a logarithmic-decay discount rate on the modified value function and, ultimately, the optimal control policy. approach has been employed to analyze structure fluctuations in nuclear collisions at various energies, specifically between 20 A GeV and 160 A GeV.  For central collisions at each energy, the average source function was calculated and its radial shape examined to investigate how it changes with energy.  Initially, at lower energies (40, 80, and 160 A GeV), the source shows an inner radius consistent with expectations from longitudinal flow, but at higher energies (1.0, 1.6, and 2.0 GeV), the inner radius increases with energy, indicating more rapid radial flow as energies rise above 1.6 GeV. a highly contagious and deadly parasite that affects honeybees worldwide, causing airway obstruction in the bee host and spreading through direct mite contact or infected mites dropping from the air. Despite existing control methods, V. destructor remains a persistent threat to global bee populations. To comprehend the mite's spread and potential outbreaks, it is essential to model its epidemiology. Existing models have been developed to predict the spread of V. destructor, but they lack the capacity to account for the impact of mites dropping from the air on the spread of the disease in neighboring areas. To address this shortfall, we have created a stochastic agent-based model to reflect this phenomenon and conducted two types of analysis: deterministic and stochastic. The results of the analysis revealed that the stochastic model exhibits periodic fluctuations in the spread of the disease, whereas the deterministic model fails to capture this fluctuation. Furthermore, the data from the Korean National Apiculture Information System, which tracks the infestation rates of V. destructor in Korea from 2000 to 2020, was used to estimate the parameters in our model. The findings from our study also identified an early warning sign for outbreaks based on the distribution of infestation rates among bee populations. To facilitate continuous monitoring of V. destructor infestations, the source code for the model is available online and includes a user-friendly interface for predicting the spread of the disease and detecting early warning signs for outbreaks. Consequently, this study has the potential to enhance the effectiveness of surveillance and outbreak prevention efforts. Additionally, the discovery of an early warning sign may contribute to fundamental knowledge about the dynamics of the V. destructor life cycle and the spread of the disease in the field. The model can be adapted to monitor the spread of other contagious and airborne parasites in the Apis mellifera population. Furthermore, the methodology employed in this study may be applicable to the detection of early warning signs in other systems exhibiting complex, stochastic dynamics. The data analyzed in the study is publicly available on the National Apiculture Information System of Korea and can be accessed via the R Shiny application included in the source code. The source code and application are designed to provide practical benefits for researchers and the apiculture community, allowing them to explore the results of the study and detect early warning signs for V. destructor outbreaks in real-time. The R Shiny application is available online, and the source code is available on GitHub. The study also presents an open-source Python application that can be accessed via the BeeOutbreaks interface, enabling the detection of early warning signs and prediction

properties of a stochastic process whose values at different times are correlated and influence one another in a memoryless manner, specifically the autoregressive process of order p. We examine how the asymptotic behavior of this process's stationary distribution is affected by the presence of negative feedback in its parameters. Two important aspects of this analysis are the short-term characteristics, which relate to the spectrum of the process, and the long-term characteristics, which relate to the distribution of the process itself. We demonstrate that the spectrum remains unchanged regardless of the feedback, whereas the distribution is heavily influenced by the feedback and even becomes multi-modal for certain parameters. This underlying structure can lead to counter-intuitive phenomena, such as the emergence of downswings even in a process with overall positive feedback. We further establish that the distribution's asymptotic behavior can be comprehensively understood through the roots of a polynomial derived from the process's parameters. This analysis provides a broad framework for examining the asymptotic properties of the autoregressive process and its numerous applications. This framework can be utilized across various contexts such as statistics and control theory. This research is also a preliminary step for exploring more complex autoregressive processes with multiple time-varying parameters. Alongside this main contribution, we offer an exploration of the related moving average process. This analysis is accompanied by numerical simulations and graphical illustrations to convey the results' significance and interpretability. in a metropolitan area in Italy, using real data from before and during the 
COVID-19 pandemic. By simulating the movement of populations in spatial networks,

greatest reduction in epidemic spread, and that targeting nodes with high 
connectivity and location can be more effective. These findings provide 
insights into designing more efficient social distancing strategies.  We further 
demonstrate that by identifying and disrupting the most critical population 
movements, one can significantly slow the epidemic spread with minimal reduction

We propose a novel form of digital coherent detection, known as the optimized delay-matched filter (ODMF), which offers superior performance to conventional techniques such as decision feedback equalization (DFE) and the optimized decision feedback equalizer (ODEQ). We demonstrate that the ODMF can be derived directly from the ideal coherent detection method and provide analytical expressions for its key performance indicators, including symbol error rate (SER) and bit error rate (BER). We also showcase as well as numerically validate the tightness of upper bounds for SER and BER when employing the ODMF. To facilitate practical implementation of the ODMF, we investigate its applicability to polarization-mode dispersion (PMDD-FDM) systems and propose an iterative technique for optimizing its delay period. We also showcase the versatility of the ODMF by integrating it with various front-end components, such as optical filter delay lines and differential group delay lines. We present numerical findings indicating that the ODMF can achieve nearly identical performance to its ideal counterpart while requiring significantly lower signal-to-noise ratios, thus conferring BER resilience up to 10 dB. We also present simulation results indicating that the ODMF can attain far superior performance to DFE and ODEQ, with gains of up to 5 dB in the waterfilling case and 2 dB in the maximum likelihood case. We further present numerical findings indicating that the tightness of the upper bound for SER and BER can be guaranteed with a cyclic prefix (CP) length as low as 80 samples, corresponding to a bandwidth efficiency of 10. Within the framework of the minimal standard model, CP symmetry is inherently broken due to the complex nature of the third generation Yukawa coupling, resulting in the average CP-violating parameter being non-zero. Consequently, the average CP-violating parameter should be approximately $\left(5.8\times10^{-6}\right)\left(\theta_{\rm CW}\right)^3$ hold true. Moreover, CP symmetry can be broken in a more extensive context where the Yukawa couplings follow a specific set of conditions, and in such a scenario, the average CP-violating parameter can take on any value within the range of $10^{-6}$ to $10^{-4}$. Furthermore, it can be demonstrated that CP symmetry can be broken to a noticeable degree without conflicting with the established limits on Yukawa couplings. Moreover, in situations where ALPs are coupled to neutrinos, the sum of the neutrino masses should be under the limit of $0.1$ eV to prevent a violation of the established limit for the CP-violating parameter by more than two orders of magnitude. On the other hand, if ALPs are coupled to the electron or the muon, the corresponding lower limits on the mass of the ALP become $10^{-2}$ eV and $10^{-3}$ eV respectively, and in such a case, a slight violation of the established limit for the CP-violating parameter can be achieved when the ALP mass is around $10^{-1}$ eV. Nevertheless, when ALPs are coupled to the top quark, the violation of the established limit for the CP-violating parameter can be achieved when the ALP mass and the phase of the CKM matrix are both large enough, and in such a scenario the sum of the neutrino masses can be as low as $0.01$ eV.

This note presents an analogous finding related to the cover time, showing that the time required to cover a graph $G$ using independent random walks from an initial set $S$ is sensitive to the distance between nodes in $G$.  Specifically, for a graph $G$ with maximum degree $\Delta$ and an initial set $S$ containing $k$ points, the cover time can be as short as $O(\Delta^2 k)$, but also exhibits a lower bound of $\Omega(k^{1/d})$ for $d$-dimensional grids, and an even more significant drop in degree for grid graphs, such as from $\Omega(\sqrt{n})$ to $\Omega(n^{1/3})$ between cover and mixing time in 3-dimensional grids.
